clinicalPearls: A neurodevelopmental disorder caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in POGZ
Developmental delay and intellectual disability are consistent, frequently with autism spectrum disorder
Behavioural features and, in some, hyperphagia with a tendency to obesity are reported
Visual problems, including refractive error and strabismus, are common
Hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and sleep disturbance may be present, especially in early childhood
Subtle and variable facial features can include a broad forehead and midface differences
Most cases arise de novo as new dominant variants
Diagnosis is established by identifying a POGZ variant through exome or gene panel testing
reference.pathophysiology: White-Sutton syndrome results from heterozygous loss-of-function variants in POGZ, which encodes a heterochromatin-associated protein containing zinc-finger domains that participates in chromatin regulation, chromosome segregation, and the control of gene transcription during neurodevelopment. By influencing the expression of genes required for the development and function of neurones, POGZ contributes to normal cognition, behaviour, and sensory processing. Reduced dosage of the protein through haploinsufficiency disrupts these processes, producing the intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, visual problems, and associated findings that characterise the syndrome. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and most cases occur as de novo events.
additionalDifferentials: Autism spectrum disorder with intellectual disability of other genetic cause
Prader-Willi and other syndromes when hyperphagia and obesity predominate
Fragile X syndrome in males with autism and intellectual disability
Copy-number neurodevelopmental syndromes identified on microarray
Other syndromic causes of hypotonia and developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Exome or gene panel testing to identify a POGZ variant
Chromosomal microarray to exclude a copy-number cause
Ophthalmological review for refractive error and strabismus
Feeding, growth, and weight monitoring, including for emerging hyperphagia
Sleep assessment where sleep disturbance is significant
redFlags: Severe feeding difficulty with faltering growth in infancy
Rapid weight gain from hyperphagia with metabolic consequences
Vision-threatening ocular problems in a young child
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is generally normal, and the long-term picture is defined by intellectual disability and autism spectrum features of variable severity together with any behavioural, visual, and weight-related issues; developmental progress is expected with educational and therapeutic support, and outcome depends chiefly on the degree of neurodevelopmental involvement.
pitfalls: Labelling the presentation as idiopathic autism and not pursuing genetic testing that would identify POGZ
Overlooking treatable visual problems that affect learning and behaviour
Failing to monitor for hyperphagia and obesity as the child grows
Assuming inheritance from a parent when most cases are de novo

management: With no disease-specific therapy available, provide early developmental intervention with speech, language and occupational therapy for delay and intellectual disability
Offer autism-specific behavioural support and educational adaptations
Arrange ophthalmological correction of refractive error and management of strabismus
Monitor feeding, growth and weight, with dietary measures to address emerging hyperphagia and obesity
Manage sleep disturbance with behavioural sleep strategies
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant condition, noting most cases are de novo, with parental testing to inform recurrence risk
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental team
